newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-PolyGram slips amid film loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-PolyGram slips amid film loss.

text.p: Music and movies group PolyGram NV -- which has a repertoire ranging from U2 to Pavarotti and is behind movie hits such as Sleepers and Train Spotting -- on Tuesday reported a dip in first quarter profits.
Making its first ever quarterly results announcement, PolyGram said a strong music performance was counterbalanced by increased operating losses in the film division.

The Dutch company, 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics NV, said first quarter 1997 net profit dipped 1.6 percent to 122 million guilders ($63.7 million) from 124 million in the first quarter of 1996.
Share analysts had anticipated net profit in the period would be flat or as high as 135 million guilders, boosted by the strong gains in the dollar and sterling against the guilder.

"The results of the music division were OK, but film was disappointing. We expected (film) losses to widen, but they really plunged," said Andre Moons of ING Barings. "There are some signs that things were improving towards the end of the first quarter and we expect this to continue in the second quarter," he added.

Net sales from the company, which also has international rock acts such as INXS and Jon Bon Jovi on its books along with mellower artists such Sheryl Crow, Elton John and Boyz II Men as well as extensive jazz and classical catalogues, climbed 8.4 percent to 2.20 billion guilders.

"PolyGram's results for the first quarter of 1997 reflect an improved contribution from music where the operating margin benefited from both international and local hits. This was offset by the expected weaker performance from film," the company said in a statement with the results.
Operating profit at the music division rose to 251 million guilders from 211 million on sales which ran up to 1.91 billion guilders from 1.74 billion.
But the film division, which released only four films in the first quarter against seven a year earlier, was hit by the underperformance of "Portrait of a Lady" and "Gridlock'd".
Operating losses at the film unit widened to 55 million guilders in the first quarter from 19 million guilders a year earlier with net sales barely increased to 293 million guilders from 287 million.

In 1996 the film business made a 35 million guilder operating loss after breaking even in the second half. PolyGram Chief Executive Alain Levy said at the full year 1996 stage that the company was not expecting a film profit in 1997.
"We are comforted by the fact that we continue to see the quality of our film product improve and our overall slate developing as planned," the results announcement said.

It added that film was weak because the release schedule was weighted to the second half of the year, but said it foresaw "satisfactory" full year results from the film division bearing in mind the start-up costs of entering U.S. mainstream theatrical distribution.
PolyGram said a stronger music release schedule contributed to sales growth of nine percent in Europe and 12 percent in North America.

The new album "Pop" from Irish rockers U2, which was delayed from last year and released in March, sold nearly five million units worldwide during the period, making it the company's best seller in the quarter.

Operating margins at the music unit, which a spokeswoman said were up to 13.1 percent in the period from 12.1 percent in the first quarter of 1996, also benefited from strong releases from the Bee Gees, Warren G and Texas, PolyGram said.
Local artists such as Andrea Bocelli in Italy and Marco Borsato in the Netherlands also made a strong contribution, with Bocelli selling over two million albums in the first quarter.
Releases from 1996 which carried over well into 1997 included albums from Sheryl Crow, Foxy Brown, Zucchero as well as soundtracks from "Grease" and "Shine".
For the remainder of 1997 PolyGram said it was expecting new albums from established artists such as Wet Wet Wet, INXS, Jon Bon Jovi, Boyz II Men and Elton John.
